tweets: Surrounded by salt desert and barely any rain, this 4,500-year-old city never went thirsty. Dholavira's builders didn't find water nearby — they engineered a way to keep every drop that fell from the sky. 💧

Dholavira sat on Khadir island in Kutch, Gujarat, boxed in by two seasonal streams, the Manhar and the Mansar. Harappan engineers dammed both, diverting monsoon runoff into the city instead of letting it vanish into the sand.

Archaeologists have found at least 16 stone-cut reservoirs inside Dholavira, some over 7m deep. Nearly a tenth of the walled city's area was reservoirs and channels — a scale of water infrastructure that's rare even in cities today.

Sluice gates, drains, and a massive stepped reservoir beside the citadel moved and filtered water through the city. A full hydraulic system, cut from rock, engineered around 2500 BCE — no perennial river required.

A Bronze Age city beat water scarcity with stone, slope, and monsoon math, 4,500 years before "sustainable design" became a buzzword. Dholavira is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
